title: Comets and Shooting Stars
summary: How comets travel around the Sun, grow glowing tails, and leave dust that lights up the night sky as shooting stars.
poll: Shooting stars are more exciting to watch than comets.

versions.title: Not a Star at All
versions.text:
Look up at night. Do you see a fast streak of light? Some call it a shooting star. But it is not a star!

It starts with a comet. A comet is a ball of ice, dust, and rock. It goes round the Sun. Its path is its orbit. Most of the time, it is far out in the dark.

A comet can come near the Sun. Then it gets warm. Some ice turns to gas. The gas and dust glow. They make a long tail. The tail points away from the Sun.

One comet comes back each 76 years. It is Halley's Comet. It will be back in 2061.

A comet drops bits of dust on its path. Earth can pass through the dust. The bits hit our air fast. They get hot. They burn. Each streak is a meteor.

Most bits are as small as sand. But a big rock can fall to the ground. Rocks like that hit the sand in Saudi Arabia. They made big holes.

In August, lots of meteors fly. Go to a dark place. The desert is good. Then look up and wait!

versions.title: Not a Star at All
versions.text:
Have you seen a quick streak of light in the night sky? People call it a shooting star. But it is not a star at all. It is a tiny bit of dust from space!

Lots of these bits come from comets. A comet is a big ball of ice, dust, and rock. It moves round the Sun on a long path. This path is called an orbit. Most of the time, a comet is far away. It is cold and dark out there.

Then a comet comes close to the Sun. It warms up. Some of its ice turns into gas. The gas and dust glow. They make a long tail. The tail points away from the Sun.

One well-known comet is Halley's Comet. It comes back about every 76 years. Its next visit will be in 2061.

A comet leaves a trail of dust on its orbit. Earth can pass through the trail. Then the bits rush into our air. They get so hot that they burn up. Each bright streak is called a meteor.

Most bits are smaller than a grain of sand. But now and then, a big rock falls all the way down. Long ago, rocks from space hit the sand in Saudi Arabia. They made big holes called the Wabar craters.

Each August, lots of meteors fill the sky. Go to a dark place, like the desert. Then look up!

versions.title: Comets and Shooting Stars
versions.text:
Have you ever seen a thin streak of light flash across the night sky? Many people call it a shooting star. But it is not a star at all. It is a tiny piece of space dust burning up high above you.

Many of these pieces come from comets. A comet is a large ball of ice, dust, and rock, a bit like a dirty snowball. It travels around the Sun on a long, stretched path called an orbit. For most of its journey, a comet is very far from the Sun. Out there, space is freezing and dark.

As a comet comes closer to the Sun, it begins to warm up. Some of its ice turns straight into gas. The gas and dust spread out and glow in the sunlight, forming a long tail. The tail always points away from the Sun, because sunlight pushes it outward.

The most famous comet is Halley's Comet. It returns about every 76 years. People last saw it in 1986, and it will come back in 2061.

A comet leaves a trail of dust along its orbit. When Earth passes through that trail, the bits rush into the air around our planet. They move at great speed. They become so hot that they burn up and glow. Each bright streak is called a meteor.

Most of these bits are smaller than a grain of sand. Once in a while, a larger rock survives the trip and lands on the ground. In the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia, rocks from space made a group of holes called the Wabar craters.

Every August, a meteor shower lights up the sky. To enjoy it, go to a dark place far from city lights, such as the desert. Then look up!

A comet leaves a trail of debris along its orbit. When Earth passes through that trail, the bits enter the atmosphere, the layer of air around our planet, at amazing speed. They become so hot that they burn up and glow. Each bright streak is called a meteor.

Most of these bits are smaller than a grain of sand. Once in a while, a larger rock survives and lands on the ground. A space rock that reaches the ground is called a meteorite. In the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia, meteorites made a group of holes called the Wabar craters.

versions.title: Comets and Shooting Stars
versions.text:
Have you ever noticed a thin streak of light flash across the night sky and disappear almost instantly? Many people call it a shooting star, although it is not actually a star at all; it is a tiny fragment of space debris disintegrating high above the ground, and its story usually begins with a comet.

A comet is a large ball of ice, dust, and rock, which is why astronomers sometimes describe it as a dirty snowball. Its solid center, called the nucleus, may be only a few kilometers wide. A comet travels around the Sun on a long, elongated path called an orbit, and for most of its journey it remains extremely distant from the Sun, in a remote region where space is freezing and completely dark.

As a comet approaches the Sun, its surface gradually warms, and some of its ice changes directly into gas without first becoming liquid, a process called sublimation. The escaping gas and dust spread outward and glow in the sunlight, producing an enormous cloud and a long, luminous tail. Interestingly, the tail always points away from the Sun, because sunlight and the solar wind continuously push it outward.

The most celebrated comet is Halley's Comet, which returns approximately every 76 years. People last observed it in 1986, and astronomers confidently expect it to reappear in 2061.

Every comet leaves a trail of debris along its orbit. Whenever Earth passes through that trail, the particles plunge into the atmosphere at tremendous velocity, and the air in front of them is compressed and heated so intensely that the particles burn up and glow. Each brilliant streak is called a meteor.

Most of these particles are smaller than a grain of sand. Occasionally, however, a larger rock survives the fiery descent and reaches the surface, and a space rock that lands on the ground is called a meteorite. In the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia, meteorites created a remarkable group of depressions known as the Wabar craters.

Every August, a meteor shower called the Perseids decorates the sky, because Earth crosses the debris of a comet named Swift-Tuttle. To appreciate it, travel somewhere dark, far from city lights, such as the open desert, and be patient while your eyes gradually adjust to the darkness.

versions.title: Comets and Shooting Stars
versions.text:
Have you ever noticed a thin streak of light flash across the night sky and disappear almost instantaneously? Many people call it a shooting star, although it is not actually a star at all. It is a tiny fragment of interplanetary debris disintegrating high above the ground, and its story usually begins with a comet.

A comet is a large ball of ice, dust, and rock, which is why astronomers occasionally describe it as a dirty snowball. Its solid center, called the nucleus, may measure only a few kilometers across. A comet travels around the Sun on a long, elongated path called an orbit, and for most of its journey it remains extraordinarily distant from the Sun, in a remote region where space is frigid and completely dark.

As a comet approaches the Sun, its surface gradually warms, and some of its ice transforms directly into gas without first becoming liquid, a process that scientists call sublimation. The escaping gas and dust spread outward and glow in the sunlight, producing an enormous cloud and a long, luminous tail. Surprisingly, the tail consistently points away from the Sun, because sunlight and the solar wind continuously push it outward, regardless of the direction in which the comet is traveling.

The most celebrated comet is Halley's Comet, which returns approximately every 76 years. People last observed it in 1986, and astronomers confidently anticipate that it will reappear in 2061.

Every comet deposits a trail of debris along its orbit. Whenever Earth passes through that trail, the particles plunge into the atmosphere at tremendous velocity, and the air in front of them is compressed and heated so intensely that the particles vaporize and glow, creating the brilliant streak that we call a meteor.

Most of these particles are considerably smaller than a grain of sand. Occasionally, however, a larger rock survives the fiery descent and reaches the surface, and a space rock that lands on the ground is called a meteorite. In the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia, meteorites created a remarkable collection of depressions known as the Wabar craters, which explorers documented during the twentieth century.

Every August, a meteor shower called the Perseids decorates the sky, because Earth crosses the debris left behind by a comet named Swift-Tuttle. To appreciate this celestial performance fully, travel somewhere dark, far from the glow of city lights, such as the open desert, and be patient while your eyes gradually adjust to the darkness.

To appreciate this celestial performance fully, travel somewhere dark, far from the artificial glow of city lights, such as the open desert, and be patient while your eyes gradually adjust to the darkness.

keyWords.definition: a piece of rock or metal from space that reaches a planet's surface
keyWords.example: Scientists cut the meteorite open to study the metals inside.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Wabar craters prove that meteorites are a serious danger to people living in the Empty Quarter.
Sublimation is the most important process in astronomy.
Comets release debris as they orbit the Sun, and that debris creates meteors in Earth's atmosphere.
Halley's Comet will produce the brightest meteor shower in history when it returns in 2061.
questions.why: The article traces how comets warm, shed gas and debris, and how Earth's passage through that debris produces meteors and occasionally meteorites.

wrong.A: The craters are an example of meteorites, and the article does not discuss danger to people.
wrong.B: Sublimation is one supporting detail, not the main point.
wrong.D: The article says Halley's Comet will return in 2061 but does not connect it to a meteor shower.

questions.stem: According to the article, how large may a comet's nucleus be?
options: Larger than Earth
Only a few kilometers across
About the size of a grain of sand
As wide as its tail
questions.why: The article states that the nucleus may measure only a few kilometers across.

wrong.A: The article never compares the nucleus with Earth.
wrong.C: Grains of sand describe meteor particles, not the nucleus.
wrong.D: The tail is described as long and enormous, much larger than the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which comet is the source of the Perseid meteor shower?
options: Halley's Comet
Wabar
Comet Perseus
Swift-Tuttle
questions.why: The article says Earth crosses the debris of a comet named Swift-Tuttle every August.

wrong.A: Halley's Comet is described separately and is not linked to the Perseids.
wrong.B: Wabar is the name of craters in Saudi Arabia.
wrong.C: No comet called Perseus is mentioned.

questions.stem: The article says the particles vaporize or burn up. Based on the context, what does vaporize mean?
options: Turn into gas
Break into larger rocks
Freeze solid
Change direction
questions.why: The intense heat destroys the particles by turning them into hot gas, which is why they glow and then disappear.

wrong.B: Heating makes particles disappear, not grow into rocks.
wrong.C: The particles are heated, not frozen.
wrong.D: Vaporizing describes a change of state, not of direction.

questions.stem: Why does a comet's tail point away from the Sun no matter which way the comet travels?
options: The comet always moves toward the Sun.
Gravity pulls the tail toward Earth.
Sunlight and the solar wind push the gas and dust outward.
The tail is frozen in one position.
questions.why: The article explains that sunlight and the solar wind continuously push the tail outward from the Sun.

wrong.A: The article says the direction of travel does not matter.
wrong.B: The article does not say Earth's gravity affects the tail.
wrong.D: The tail is made of escaping gas and dust, not frozen material.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the fact that most meteor particles are smaller than a grain of sand?
options: Meteors are usually much too faint for people to see without a telescope.
Even very small particles can create a bright streak because of their speed.
Most meteorites are found in deserts.
Comets are mostly made of sand.
questions.why: The article calls meteors brilliant streaks, so tiny particles must glow brightly because they hit the atmosphere at tremendous velocity.

wrong.A: The article describes meteors as brilliant, so they can be seen.
wrong.C: The article mentions one desert crater site but does not make this claim.
wrong.D: Comets are made of ice, dust, and rock, not mostly sand.

questions.stem: Why do so few meteors become meteorites?
options: Most particles are too small to survive the heat of entry.
Meteorites can only land in deserts.
Comets stop shedding debris near Earth.
The solar wind pushes them back into space.
questions.why: Most particles vaporize in the atmosphere; only a larger rock occasionally survives the fiery descent to reach the ground.

wrong.B: Meteorites can land anywhere; the Wabar craters are only one example.
wrong.C: The article says comets leave debris all along their orbits.
wrong.D: The solar wind is linked to comet tails, not to falling meteors.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the Wabar craters in the Empty Quarter?
options: To argue that the desert is a dangerous place for people to visit at night
To compare Saudi Arabia's craters with the Moon's
To explain how comets form tails
To give a real local example of meteorites reaching the ground
questions.why: After defining a meteorite, the author points to the Wabar craters as evidence of meteorites striking Saudi Arabia.

wrong.A: The article actually recommends the desert for watching meteors.
wrong.B: The Moon's craters are not mentioned.
wrong.C: Tails are explained in an earlier paragraph and are not connected to the craters.

HIGH.prompt: Trace the journey of a single dust particle from a comet's nucleus to a streak of light in Earth's sky. Use precise evidence from the article for each stage.
checklist: I described each stage of the journey in the correct order.
I used precise evidence and vocabulary from the article.
I explained what causes each change along the way.
